topics.title: Greek roots 2: rule, form, light and stars
topics.intro: More Greek building blocks: arche (rule), nomos (law), morphe (shape), phos (light), aster (star), kryptos (hidden). Many of them are words you will meet in your Greek lessons.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find a word with “-archy” or “-nomy” in the news and decode it.
topics.hook: Greek roots click together like building bricks: astron (star) + nomos (law) = astronomy.

topics.title: Greek prefixes
topics.intro: Greek prefixes change a word’s meaning at a stroke: eu- (good), dys- (bad), hyper- (over), hypo- (under), syn- (together), pan- (all), meta- (beyond).
topics.talk: Play “prefix tennis”: one of you names a Greek prefix, the other gives a word that uses it.
topics.hook: One Greek prefix can flip a word: euphoria feels good; dysfunction works badly.

topics.title: More Latin roots
topics.intro: More Latin roots that run through English: vid (see), mit (send), duc (lead), voc (call), vert (turn), loqu (speak), mort (death), omni (all).
topics.teach: Use roots to explain what “loquacious” and “omnivore” mean.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many words {she} can make from “duct” or “vert” in a minute.
topics.hook: Vid, voc, vert, mort: Latin roots hide inside words you use every day.

topics.title: Literary vocabulary
topics.intro: Words for describing characters, settings and moods precisely: foreboding, desolate, enigmatic, malevolent, capricious. The right word does the work of a whole sentence.
topics.teach: Describe a Greek god using three of today’s words, and justify each.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which of today’s words best describes {her} favourite fictional villain.
topics.hook: One precise mood word does the work of a sentence: desolate, foreboding, serene.

topics.title: Academic vocabulary for essays
topics.intro: Essay words help you argue with precision: concede, corroborate, implicit, nuanced, plausible, substantiate. They mark the difference between a good answer and an excellent one.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between “explicit” and “implicit”, with an example from a text.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to use “concede” and “however” in one spoken sentence about a family argument.
topics.hook: Essay words are the tools of argument: concede, corroborate, substantiate.

topics.title: Words easily confused
topics.intro: Affect or effect? Imply or infer? Fewer or less? Some pairs trip up adult writers. Knowing them is a quick win in every piece of writing.
topics.talk: Spot a “less” that should be “fewer” on a supermarket sign together.
topics.hook: RAVEN: Remember, Affect is a Verb, Effect is a Noun.

topics.title: Grammar for effect
topics.intro: Grammar is a toolkit for meaning: noun phrases that pack in detail, apposition, non-finite clauses, inversion, minor sentences and lists with or without “and”.
topics.teach: Explain the effect of starting a sentence with “Into the darkness crept…”.
topics.talk: Read a paragraph from {her} book together and find one sentence built for effect.
topics.hook: Grammar is a camera: it decides what the reader sees first and what comes last.

topics.title: Narrative techniques
topics.intro: Writers plan effects across a whole story: pathetic fallacy, motifs, foreshadowing, flashbacks, dramatic irony and cyclical structure. Homer used several of them nearly three thousand years ago.
topics.teach: Explain what foreshadowing is and give an example from a myth you know.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which technique the last film you watched together used.
topics.hook: Plant, then pay off: foreshadowing, motifs and echoes make a story feel designed.

topics.title: Writing description
topics.intro: Good description is designed like a film: wide shot, zoom in, one telling detail. Precise nouns and verbs beat strings of adjectives, and every sense counts.
topics.teach: Explain why “the oak groaned” is stronger than “the big old tree made a noise”.
topics.talk: Describe the view from a window together using one sound, one smell and one texture.
topics.hook: Wide shot, close-up, one telling detail: describe like a film director.

topics.title: Non-fiction forms
topics.intro: Articles, letters, speeches, reviews and reports each have conventions. Exam tasks reward the right form for the audience and purpose.
topics.teach: Explain when you would sign a letter “Yours faithfully” rather than “Yours sincerely”.
topics.talk: Look at a newspaper together and find the headline, standfirst and byline.
topics.hook: PAF: Purpose, Audience, Form. Know all three before you write a word.

topics.title: Hard spellings
topics.intro: Words that catch out confident writers: conscientious, supersede, minuscule, manoeuvre. Each has a trick.
topics.talk: Test {him} on three of today’s words; then let {him} test you.
topics.hook: Spell the hard ones in chunks: con-sci-en-tious, man-oeu-vre.

topics.title: Narrative voice and irony
topics.intro: At GCSE you analyse how a story is told: who sees, who speaks, and how far we can trust them. Irony, free indirect style and epistolary form are the advanced tools.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between dramatic irony and situational irony.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether the narrator of {her} current book can be trusted, and why.
topics.hook: Who sees, who speaks, and can we trust them?

topics.title: Analysing structure
topics.intro: Structure questions ask why the writer arranged the text this way: shifts in focus, withheld information, changes in pace, an ending that echoes the opening.
topics.teach: Explain one structural feature in the opening of a story you know.
topics.talk: After a film, ask {him} why it began where it did.
topics.hook: Structure is the order of the reveal: what the writer shows first, shows last, and holds back.

topics.title: Advanced rhetoric
topics.intro: The Greeks taught rhetoric as an art. Beyond the rule of three: chiasmus, epistrophe, hypophora, litotes, zeugma, procatalepsis. Recognise them in great speeches and use them in your own.
topics.teach: Explain chiasmus using a famous example.
topics.talk: Listen to a short speech together and count the rhetorical devices.
topics.hook: The Greeks had a name for every trick: chiasmus, litotes, zeugma.

items.prompt: The Greek root “arche (-archy)” (as in monarchy, anarchy) means…
items.explain: arche (-archy): rule or chief. Think of monarchy.
items.hook: An archbishop is a chief bishop; an archenemy is your chief enemy.
items.example: Monarchy is rule by one (monos); anarchy is having no ruler at all.

items.prompt: The Greek root “nomos (-nomy)” (as in astronomy, autonomy) means…
items.explain: nomos (-nomy): law or arrangement. Think of astronomy.
items.example: Astronomy is the “law of the stars”: astron (star) + nomos (law).

items.prompt: The Greek root “kinesis (kine-)” (as in kinetic, cinema) means…
items.explain: kinesis (kine-): movement. Think of kinetic.
items.example: Cinema comes from kinema, movement: a cinema shows moving pictures.

items.prompt: The Greek root “morphe (morph-)” (as in metamorphosis, amorphous) means…
items.explain: morphe (morph-): form or shape. Think of metamorphosis.
items.example: A caterpillar turning into a butterfly is a metamorphosis: a change of shape.

items.prompt: The Greek root “phos (photo-)” (as in photograph, photosynthesis) means…
items.explain: phos (photo-): light. Think of photograph.
items.example: Phosphorus glows in the dark: its name means “light-bringer”.

items.prompt: The Greek root “pseudo-” (as in pseudonym, pseudoscience) means…
items.explain: pseudo-: false. Think of pseudonym.
items.example: Mary Ann Evans wrote her novels under a pseudonym (false name): George Eliot.

items.prompt: The Greek root “xenos (xeno-)” (as in xenophobia) means…
items.explain: xenos (xeno-): stranger or foreign. Think of xenophobia.
items.hook: Xenia was the Greek law of hospitality to strangers, and Zeus himself protected guests.

items.prompt: The Greek root “kryptos (crypto-)” (as in cryptic, cryptography) means…
items.explain: kryptos (crypto-): hidden. Think of cryptic.
items.example: A crypt is a hidden room beneath a church.

items.prompt: The Greek root “chroma (chrom-)” (as in chromatic, monochrome) means…
items.explain: chroma (chrom-): colour. Think of chromatic.
items.hook: Chromosomes are “coloured bodies”: they were named because they soak up coloured dyes.
items.example: A monochrome photo uses shades of just one colour.

items.prompt: The Greek root “derma (derm-)” (as in dermatology, epidermis) means…
items.explain: derma (derm-): skin. Think of dermatology.
items.example: A dermatologist is a skin doctor; a hypodermic needle goes under the skin.

items.prompt: The Greek root “kosmos (cosm-)” (as in cosmos, cosmopolitan) means…
items.explain: kosmos (cosm-): order or the world. Think of cosmos.
items.hook: Kosmos meant order and ornament: cosmetics, which make you look neat and beautiful, share the root.

items.prompt: The Greek root “aster (astr-)” (as in astronomy, asteroid) means…
items.explain: aster (astr-): star. Think of astronomy.
items.example: An asterisk (*) is a “little star”; an astronaut is a “star sailor”.

items.prompt: The Greek root “kyklos (cycl-)” (as in cycle, encyclopedia) means…
items.explain: kyklos (cycl-): circle or wheel. Think of cycle.
items.example: A bicycle has two wheels; a cyclone is a storm that whirls round in a circle.

items.prompt: The Greek root “genos (gen-)” (as in genesis, genetics) means…
items.explain: genos (gen-): birth, kind or origin. Think of genesis.
items.example: Genesis, the first book of the Bible, tells of the beginning of the world.

items.prompt: The Greek root “hemi-” (as in hemisphere) means…
items.explain: hemi-: half. Think of hemisphere.
items.example: The equator splits the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres.

items.prompt: The Greek root “isos (iso-)” (as in isosceles, isobar) means…
items.explain: isos (iso-): equal. Think of isosceles.
items.example: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides: isos (equal) + skelos (leg).

items.prompt: Using Greek roots, what is “cryptography”?

options.text: the study of secret writing and codes
the study of how crystals form
options.feedback: kryptos means hidden; graphein means to write.
A crypt is a hidden room, but cryptography is about secret writing.

items.explain: kryptos (hidden) + graphein (to write): writing in code.
items.example: In the Second World War, codebreakers at Bletchley Park cracked enemy codes.

items.prompt: A country with “autonomy” has…

options.text: no laws at all, only customs
options.feedback: That would be anarchy.

options.text: a king chosen by the people
options.feedback: That is a monarchy.

items.explain: autos (self) + nomos (law).
items.example: Scotland and Wales have their own parliaments, with some autonomy from Westminster.

items.prompt: What is an “isobar” on a weather map?

options.text: a line joining places of equal air pressure
a line joining places of equal temperature
options.feedback: That is an isotherm.

options.text: a line showing the edge of an island
options.feedback: iso- means equal, not island.

items.explain: isos (equal) + baros (weight, pressure).
items.example: On a TV weather map, isobars packed close together mean strong winds.

items.prompt: Using roots, “amorphous” describes something…

options.feedback: amor is Latin for love; this is Greek a- (without) + morphe (shape).
morphe means shape, not morning.

items.explain: a- (without) + morphe (shape).
items.hook: A- (without) + morphe (shape): amorphous means shapeless, like a blob of jelly.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “dys-” (as in dysfunction, dystopia) means…
items.explain: dys-: bad or difficult. Think of dysfunction.
items.example: Dystopian novels imagine a terrible future society, like Orwell’s Nineteen Eighty-Four.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “eu-” (as in euphoria, euphemism) means…
items.explain: eu-: good or well. Think of euphoria.
items.hook: Eu- = good: euphoria is feeling good; a euphemism is a nicer way of saying something.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “hetero-” (as in heterogeneous) means…
items.explain: hetero-: other or different. Think of heterogeneous.
items.example: A bowl of mixed nuts is heterogeneous; a glass of milk looks homogeneous.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “homo-” (as in homogeneous, homophone) means…
items.explain: homo-: same. Think of homogeneous.
items.hook: Homophones sound the same: there, their, they’re.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “mega-” (as in megaphone, megalith) means…
items.explain: mega-: great or large. Think of megaphone.
items.example: A megaphone makes your voice great and loud; the stones of Stonehenge are megaliths.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “meta-” (as in metaphor, metamorphosis) means…
items.explain: meta-: after, beyond or change. Think of metaphor.
items.example: A tadpole turning into a frog is a metamorphosis: a change of form.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “para-” (as in parallel, paradox) means…
items.explain: para-: beside or beyond. Think of parallel.
items.hook: Para = beside: parallel lines run beside each other for ever.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “peri-” (as in perimeter, periscope) means…
items.explain: peri-: around. Think of perimeter.
items.example: A perimeter fence runs all the way around the edge of a site.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “pan-” (as in panorama, pandemic) means…
items.explain: pan-: all. Think of panorama.
items.example: A panorama shows all of a view; a pandemic spreads among all the people.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “syn- / sym-” (as in synthesis, symphony) means…
items.explain: syn- / sym-: together or with. Think of synthesis.
items.hook: Syn = together: a symphony is sounds together; synchronised swimmers move together.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “hyper-” (as in hyperactive, hyperbole) means…
items.explain: hyper-: over, above or excessive. Think of hyperactive.
items.example: A hypermarket is a supermarket that is extra large.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “hypo-” (as in hypothermia, hypodermic) means…
items.explain: hypo-: under or below. Think of hypothermia.
items.hook: Hypo = under: in hypothermia, your body heat falls under normal.
items.example: Mountain rescue teams warn winter walkers about hypothermia.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “mono-” (as in monologue, monotheism) means…
items.explain: mono-: one or alone. Think of monologue.
items.example: A monorail runs on one rail; a monologue is one person speaking.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “neo-” (as in neon, Neolithic) means…
items.explain: neo-: new. Think of neon.
items.example: Neon was named “the new one” when it was discovered in 1898.

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “ortho-” (as in orthodontist, orthodox) means…
items.explain: ortho-: straight or correct. Think of orthodontist.
items.example: An orthodontist straightens teeth: ortho (straight) + odous (tooth).

items.prompt: The Greek prefix “a- / an-” (as in atheist, anonymous) means…
items.explain: a- / an-: not or without. Think of atheist.
items.hook: A- or an- = without: anonymous means without a name (onoma).

items.prompt: A “dystopia” is…

options.text: an imagined society where everything is bad
an imagined society where everything is perfect
options.feedback: That is a utopia: dys- means bad.

options.text: a society split into two warring sides
options.feedback: dys- means bad or difficult, not two.

items.explain: dys- (bad) + topos (place). Utopia was coined from ou (no) + topos: nowhere.
items.hook: Thomas More’s Utopia (1516) described an ideal island whose name means “no place”.

items.prompt: A “eulogy” is…

options.text: a speech praising someone, often at a funeral
a cruel insult spoken behind someone’s back
options.feedback: eu- means good.

options.text: a scientific study of how people speak
options.feedback: logos here means words, not study.

items.explain: eu- (good) + logos (word): speaking well of someone.
items.example: At funerals, someone often gives a eulogy: a speech in praise of the person who has died.

items.prompt: A “panacea” is supposed to be…

options.text: a type of flat Greek bread
options.feedback: pan- here is Greek “all”.

options.text: a mild illness that soon passes
options.feedback: akos means remedy.

items.explain: pan- (all) + akos (cure). Panakeia was a Greek goddess of healing.
items.example: People say “there is no panacea” for a complicated problem: no single cure-all.

items.prompt: If a group is “heterogeneous”, its members are…

options.text: all the same as each other
options.feedback: That is homogeneous.
genos means kind; hetero- means different.

items.explain: hetero- (other, different) + genos (kind).

items.prompt: The Latin root “vid / vis” (as in video, visible) means…
items.explain: vid / vis: see. Think of video.
items.example: Video is Latin for “I see”.

items.prompt: The Latin root “mit / miss” (as in transmit, mission) means…
items.explain: mit / miss: send. Think of transmit.
items.example: A missile is sent through the air; a mission is a task you are sent on.

items.prompt: The Latin root “duc / duct” (as in conduct, educate) means…
items.explain: duc / duct: lead. Think of conduct.
items.example: An aqueduct leads water: aqua (water) + ducere (to lead).

items.prompt: The Latin root “voc / vok” (as in vocal, provoke) means…
items.explain: voc / vok: call or voice. Think of vocal.
items.example: Your vocal cords make your voice; an advocate is someone called in to speak for you.

items.prompt: The Latin root “fract / frag” (as in fraction, fragile) means…
items.explain: fract / frag: break. Think of fraction.
items.example: A fracture is a broken bone; a fraction is a broken-off part of a whole.

items.prompt: The Latin root “pend / pens” (as in pendulum, suspend) means…
items.explain: pend / pens: hang or weigh. Think of pendulum.
items.example: A pendant hangs from a chain; a pendulum hangs and swings.

items.prompt: The Latin root “sci” (as in science, conscious) means…
items.explain: sci: know. Think of science.
items.example: Science is knowledge; to be conscious is to know what is going on around you.

items.prompt: The Latin root “tract” (as in tractor, attract) means…
items.explain: tract: pull or draw. Think of tractor.
items.example: A tractor pulls a plough; a magnet attracts, pulling things towards it.

items.prompt: The Latin root “vert / vers” (as in reverse, convert) means…
items.explain: vert / vers: turn. Think of reverse.
items.example: An introvert turns inwards; an extrovert turns outwards; vertigo makes the world seem to spin.

items.prompt: The Latin root “cap / capt” (as in capture, captive) means…
items.explain: cap / capt: take or seize. Think of capture.
items.example: A captor takes a captive; a captivating story seizes your attention.

items.prompt: The Latin root “fac / fic” (as in factory, efficient) means…
items.explain: fac / fic: make or do. Think of factory.
items.example: A factory is where things are made; a fact was once “a thing done”.

items.prompt: The Latin root “loqu / locut” (as in eloquent, loquacious) means…
items.explain: loqu / locut: speak. Think of eloquent.
items.example: A ventriloquist “speaks from the belly”: venter (belly) + loqui (to speak).

items.prompt: The Latin root “mort” (as in mortal, mortuary) means…
items.explain: mort: death. Think of mortal.
items.example: Mortgage comes from Old French for a “death pledge”.

items.prompt: The Latin root “nov” (as in novel, renovate) means…
items.explain: nov: new. Think of novel.
items.example: A novice is new to something; to renovate a house is to make it new again.

items.prompt: The Latin root “omni” (as in omnivore, omnipotent) means…
items.explain: omni: all. Think of omnivore.
items.example: An omnibus was a coach “for all”: that is where the word bus comes from.

items.prompt: The Latin root “ambi” (as in ambidextrous, ambiguous) means…
items.explain: ambi: both. Think of ambidextrous.
items.hook: Ambi = both: ambidextrous (both hands), ambiguous (both ways), ambivalent (both feelings).

items.prompt: A “loquacious” person…

options.feedback: loqu means speak.
Think of eloquent.

items.explain: loqu (speak): a loquacious person never stops talking.
items.hook: Loquacious people love to speak; eloquent people speak well.

items.prompt: An “omnivore” eats…

options.feedback: That is a carnivore.
That is a herbivore.

items.explain: omni (all) + vorare (to swallow).
items.example: Humans, bears and pigs are omnivores: they eat both plants and meat.

items.prompt: Using roots, what does “ambidextrous” mean?

options.text: able to use both hands equally well
very skilful with the right hand
options.feedback: ambi means both.
Think of ambiguous: two meanings.

items.explain: ambi (both) + dexter (right hand): both hands as skilled as a right hand.
items.hook: Dexter = right (as in dexterity); sinister was Latin for left.

items.prompt: What does “melancholy” mean?
items.explain: melancholy: a deep, lasting sadness. A melancholy silence hung over Ithaca while its king was gone.
items.learn:
**melancholy**: a deep, lasting sadness.
_A melancholy silence hung over Ithaca while its king was gone._
items.hook: Melancholy is Greek for “black bile”, once thought to cause sadness.

items.prompt: What does “foreboding” mean?
items.answer: a feeling that something bad is about to happen
distractors: a hopeful promise that all will be well
an act that the law strictly forbids
a long, tiring wait for good news
items.explain: foreboding: a feeling that something bad is about to happen. Kit felt a chill of foreboding as the oracle fell silent.
items.learn:
**foreboding**: a feeling that something bad is about to happen.
_Kit felt a chill of foreboding as the oracle fell silent._
items.hook: Fore (before) + bode (to foretell): a warning feeling before something bad.

items.prompt: What does “desolate” mean?
items.explain: desolate: empty, bleak and lonely. The island was desolate: no trees, no birds, no people.
items.learn:
**desolate**: empty, bleak and lonely.
_The island was desolate: no trees, no birds, no people._
items.hook: Desolate comes from Latin solus, alone: a place that leaves you all alone.

items.prompt: What does “eloquent” mean?
items.answer: fluent and persuasive in speech or writing
distractors: very elegant and graceful to look at
speaking too quietly to be heard clearly
items.explain: eloquent: fluent and persuasive in speech or writing. Odysseus was famous for his eloquent speeches.
items.learn:
**eloquent**: fluent and persuasive in speech or writing.
_Odysseus was famous for his eloquent speeches._
items.hook: E (out) + loqui (to speak): words flowing out beautifully.

items.prompt: What does “enigmatic” mean?
items.explain: enigmatic: mysterious and hard to understand. The Sphinx gave an enigmatic smile.
items.learn:
**enigmatic**: mysterious and hard to understand.
_The Sphinx gave an enigmatic smile._
items.example: The smile of the Mona Lisa is often called enigmatic.

items.prompt: What does “ethereal” mean?
items.answer: delicate and light, as if unearthly
items.explain: ethereal: delicate and light, as if unearthly. An ethereal glow surrounded the goddess.
items.learn:
**ethereal**: delicate and light, as if unearthly.
_An ethereal glow surrounded the goddess._
items.hook: From ether, the pure upper air where the Greeks imagined the gods lived.

items.prompt: What does “languid” mean?
distractors: eager, lively and full of energy
items.explain: languid: relaxed, slow and lacking energy. The lotus-eaters lay in a languid daze.
items.learn:
**languid**: relaxed, slow and lacking energy.
_The lotus-eaters lay in a languid daze._
items.hook: Languid shares a Latin root with “languish”: drooping, slow, without energy.

items.prompt: What does “malevolent” mean?
items.explain: malevolent: wishing harm to others. Hera’s malevolent gaze followed Heracles everywhere.
items.learn:
**malevolent**: wishing harm to others.
_Hera’s malevolent gaze followed Heracles everywhere._
items.hook: Mal (bad) + volent (wishing): wishing harm. Its opposite is benevolent.

items.prompt: What does “petulant” mean?
distractors: covered in petals, like a flower
brave in the face of danger
items.explain: petulant: childishly sulky or bad-tempered. Achilles sat in his tent, petulant and proud.
items.learn:
**petulant**: childishly sulky or bad-tempered.
_Achilles sat in his tent, petulant and proud._
items.example: A toddler stamping her feet because she cannot have sweets is being petulant.

items.prompt: What does “resolute” mean?
items.explain: resolute: determined and unwavering. Penelope remained resolute, refusing every suitor.
items.learn:
**resolute**: determined and unwavering.
_Penelope remained resolute, refusing every suitor._
items.hook: Resolute = full of resolve: like a New Year’s resolution you actually keep.

items.prompt: What does “sardonic” mean?
items.explain: sardonic: grimly mocking or cynical. Hermes gave a sardonic laugh at the mortals’ plans.
items.learn:
**sardonic**: grimly mocking or cynical.
_Hermes gave a sardonic laugh at the mortals’ plans._
items.example: A sardonic remark: “Oh, wonderful. Another Monday.”

items.prompt: What does “serene” mean?
items.explain: serene: calm and peaceful. The sea lay serene after the storm.
items.learn:
**serene**: calm and peaceful.
_The sea lay serene after the storm._
items.example: “Serene Highness” is still the formal style of the Prince of Monaco.

items.prompt: What does “tenacious” mean?
distractors: tense and nervous before a test
easily giving up when things get hard
items.explain: tenacious: holding on firmly; persistent. The tenacious hero clung to the ram’s fleece.
items.learn:
**tenacious**: holding on firmly; persistent.
_The tenacious hero clung to the ram’s fleece._
items.hook: Latin tenere, to hold: tenacious means you hold on, like a terrier with a stick.

items.prompt: What does “visceral” mean?
items.answer: felt deep in the body; instinctive
items.explain: visceral: felt deep in the body; instinctive. The roar of the Minotaur produced a visceral terror.
items.learn:
**visceral**: felt deep in the body; instinctive.
_The roar of the Minotaur produced a visceral terror._
items.hook: The viscera are the guts: a visceral feeling hits you in the stomach.

items.prompt: What does “indomitable” mean?
items.explain: indomitable: impossible to defeat or subdue. Her indomitable spirit carried her through the labyrinth.
items.learn:
**indomitable**: impossible to defeat or subdue.
_Her indomitable spirit carried her through the labyrinth._
items.hook: In (not) + domitable (tameable): impossible to tame.

items.prompt: What does “capricious” mean?
items.explain: capricious: changing mood suddenly and unpredictably. The capricious gods rewarded one hero and ruined the next.
items.learn:
**capricious**: changing mood suddenly and unpredictably.
_The capricious gods rewarded one hero and ruined the next._
items.example: British weather is famously capricious: sun, hail and rain in one afternoon.

items.prompt: What does “ambivalent” mean?
distractors: able to use both hands equally well
items.explain: ambivalent: having mixed feelings about something. Readers are often ambivalent about Achilles: brave, but cruel.
items.learn:
**ambivalent**: having mixed feelings about something.
_Readers are often ambivalent about Achilles: brave, but cruel._
items.hook: Ambi (both) + valent (strong): two strong feelings pulling both ways.

items.prompt: What does “coherent” mean?
items.explain: coherent: logical and consistent. A coherent essay builds one argument step by step.
items.learn:
**coherent**: logical and consistent.
_A coherent essay builds one argument step by step._
items.hook: Latin co (together) + haerere (to stick): a coherent argument sticks together.

items.prompt: What does “concede” mean?
items.answer: to admit, often reluctantly, that something is true
distractors: to hide the truth from someone
to win an argument by persuasion
items.explain: concede: to admit, often reluctantly, that something is true. I concede that Sparta’s army was stronger, but Athens had the navy.
items.learn:
**concede**: to admit, often reluctantly, that something is true.
_I concede that Sparta’s army was stronger, but Athens had the navy._
items.example: Losing candidates concede defeat on election night: they admit the other side has won.

items.prompt: What does “contentious” mean?
items.explain: contentious: likely to cause argument. Returning the Parthenon Marbles is a contentious issue.
items.learn:
**contentious**: likely to cause argument.
_Returning the Parthenon Marbles is a contentious issue._
items.hook: Contentious contains “content”, but think of “contend”: likely to start a contest of opinions.

items.prompt: What does “corroborate” mean?
distractors: to work together on a project
items.explain: corroborate: to confirm with further evidence. Archaeology can corroborate parts of Homer’s story.
items.learn:
**corroborate**: to confirm with further evidence.
_Archaeology can corroborate parts of Homer’s story._
items.hook: Corroborate = check it with a co-witness: do other sources agree?
items.example: Detectives corroborate an alibi by checking CCTV or asking other witnesses.

items.prompt: What does “empirical” mean?
distractors: to do with empires and emperors
items.explain: empirical: based on observation or experiment. Aristotle collected empirical evidence by dissecting animals.
items.learn:
**empirical**: based on observation or experiment.
_Aristotle collected empirical evidence by dissecting animals._
items.hook: Empirical comes from Greek empeiria, experience: test it and see.

items.prompt: What does “explicit” mean?
items.explain: explicit: stated clearly and directly. The oracle never gave an explicit answer.
items.learn:
**explicit**: stated clearly and directly.
_The oracle never gave an explicit answer._
items.hook: Explicit = folded out, in the open (ex = out). Implicit = folded in (im = in).

items.prompt: What does “implicit” mean?
items.explain: implicit: suggested but not stated directly. There is an implicit warning in the myth of Icarus.
items.learn:
**implicit**: suggested but not stated directly.
_There is an implicit warning in the myth of Icarus._
items.example: “Is that your coat on the floor?” carries an implicit instruction: pick it up.

items.prompt: What does “inherent” mean?
items.answer: existing as a natural, permanent part
items.explain: inherent: existing as a natural, permanent part. Risk is inherent in any sea voyage.
items.learn:
**inherent**: existing as a natural, permanent part.
_Risk is inherent in any sea voyage._
items.hook: In + haerere (to stick): an inherent quality is stuck inside the thing itself.

items.prompt: What does “mitigate” mean?
distractors: to move away to another place
items.explain: mitigate: to make something less severe. Sea walls can mitigate the damage done by storms.
items.learn:
**mitigate**: to make something less severe.
_Sea walls can mitigate the damage done by storms._
items.example: In court, a lawyer may point to mitigating circumstances to reduce a sentence.

items.prompt: What does “nuanced” mean?
items.explain: nuanced: showing subtle shades of meaning. Her answer was nuanced: Odysseus is both clever and cruel.
items.learn:
**nuanced**: showing subtle shades of meaning.
_Her answer was nuanced: Odysseus is both clever and cruel._
items.hook: Nuance comes from French for a shade of colour: a nuanced view sees the shades, not just black and white.

items.prompt: What does “pervasive” mean?
items.explain: pervasive: spreading widely throughout. A pervasive sense of doom fills the play.
items.learn:
**pervasive**: spreading widely throughout.
_A pervasive sense of doom fills the play._
items.hook: Pervasive things pervade, spreading through everything, like the smell of toast through a house.

items.prompt: What does “plausible” mean?
items.explain: plausible: seeming reasonable or likely. It is plausible that a real war lies behind the Iliad.
items.learn:
**plausible**: seeming reasonable or likely.
_It is plausible that a real war lies behind the Iliad._
items.hook: Plausible comes from Latin for “deserving applause”: an idea that wins a nod.

items.prompt: What does “scrutinise” mean?
items.explain: scrutinise: to examine very closely. Historians scrutinise every source for bias.
items.learn:
**scrutinise**: to examine very closely.
_Historians scrutinise every source for bias._
items.example: Referees scrutinise video replays; proofreaders scrutinise every line.

items.prompt: What does “substantiate” mean?
items.answer: to support a claim with evidence
distractors: to make heavier or more solid
items.explain: substantiate: to support a claim with evidence. You must substantiate every point with a quotation.
items.learn:
**substantiate**: to support a claim with evidence.
_You must substantiate every point with a quotation._
items.hook: Substantiate = give your claim substance: evidence that makes it solid.

items.prompt: What does “tentative” mean?
distractors: a temporary shelter, like a tent
items.explain: tentative: not certain or fixed; hesitant. She offered a tentative interpretation of the riddle.
items.learn:
**tentative**: not certain or fixed; hesitant.
_She offered a tentative interpretation of the riddle._
items.example: A tentative first step on to ice: careful, unsure, ready to pull back.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The storm will ___ the harvest.”

options.feedback: “effect” is usually a noun: the effect of the storm.

items.explain: Affect is usually a verb (to influence); effect is usually a noun (a result). RAVEN: Remember, Affect Verb, Effect Noun.
items.example: A forecast might warn that snow will affect travel; the effect is often long delays.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The ___ of the plague on Athens was devastating.”

options.feedback: Here we need a noun: the result.

items.explain: The effect (noun) of the plague.
items.hook: Affect = Action; Effect = End result.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “From her silence, Kit ___ that something was wrong.”

options.feedback: Kit is the listener working it out, so he infers. The speaker implies.

items.explain: Speakers and writers imply; listeners and readers infer.
items.hook: The speaker implies (puts it in); the listener infers (takes it out).

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The oracle ___ that the voyage would end badly, though she never said it outright.”

options.feedback: The oracle is the speaker, hinting: she implies.

items.explain: To imply is to suggest without saying directly.
items.example: “Some of us did our homework” implies that someone did not.

items.prompt: Which is correct?

options.text: The fleet comprises of twelve ships.
options.feedback: Comprise never takes “of”. Use “consists of” or “is composed of”.

options.text: The fleet is comprising of twelve ships.
options.feedback: No “of” after comprise.

items.explain: Comprise means “consist of”, so “comprises of” doubles up.
items.hook: Comprise = includes. You would never say “includes of”, so never “comprises of”.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “___ people came to the festival this year.”

options.feedback: People can be counted, so use fewer.

items.explain: Fewer for things you can count; less for amounts you cannot (less water, fewer cups).
items.example: Food labels need both words: fewer calories, less sugar.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “There was ___ water in the well than last summer.”

options.feedback: Water cannot be counted one by one, so use less.

items.explain: Less for uncountable amounts.
items.hook: Less for a heap (water, time, money); fewer for a count (cups, minutes, coins).

items.prompt: A judge in a competition should be “disinterested”. What does that mean?

options.text: impartial: she gains nothing from the result
bored and not really paying attention
options.feedback: That is “uninterested”.
The prefix dis- here means not having a personal stake.

items.explain: Disinterested = impartial; uninterested = not interested.
items.example: A referee should be disinterested (impartial), but never uninterested in the match.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses “literally” in its precise meaning?

options.text: The statue was literally made of bronze.

options.feedback: You did not actually die: this is exaggeration, not literal truth.

options.text: The exam was literally a mountain.
options.feedback: It was not actually a mountain.

items.explain: Literally means “actually, in the exact sense of the words”. Careful writers avoid it as an intensifier.
items.example: Dictionaries now also record “literally” as an intensifier, but careful writers still avoid it.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Her red scarf ___ her dark coat.”

options.feedback: A compliment is praise. Complement means goes well with or completes.

items.explain: Complement (completes, goes well with); compliment (praise).
items.hook: A complement with an e completes; a compliment with an i says “I like your scarf”.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The ___ reason for the war was control of trade.”

options.feedback: A principle is a belief or rule. Principal means main.

items.explain: Principal = main (or head of a school); principle = a rule or belief.
items.hook: The principal is your pal: the main one. A principle is a rule.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “She bought new ___ for school: pens, paper and a ruler.”

options.feedback: Stationary means not moving. Stationery (with e) is paper and pens: e for envelope.

items.explain: Stationery: e for envelope. Stationary: a for “at rest”.
items.hook: Stationery has er, as in paper; stationary has ar, as in a parked car.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The spy was ___: nobody noticed her at all.”

options.feedback: Discrete means separate and distinct, as in discrete data.

items.explain: Discreet = careful not to attract attention; discrete = separate.
items.hook: In discrete, the t keeps the two e’s separate.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “The teacher tried to ___ an answer from the class.”

options.feedback: Illicit means illegal or forbidden.

items.explain: Elicit = draw out; illicit = not allowed.
items.hook: Elicit = draw out (e = out); illicit sounds like ill: not allowed.

items.prompt: In British English, which is correct?

options.text: You need to practise every day.
You need to practice every day.
options.feedback: In British English, practice is the noun and practise the verb.

items.explain: Like advice (noun) and advise (verb): practice (noun), practise (verb).
items.hook: Advice (noun) and advise (verb) work the same way: practice (noun), practise (verb).

items.prompt: Which is correct in formal writing?

options.feedback: After a preposition, use the object form: whom.

items.explain: Whom is the object form (like him); who is the subject form (like he).
items.hook: Answer the question: if the answer is “him”, write whom. With him → with whom.

items.prompt: Which fits? “Take a warm drink, ___ tea or cocoa.” (giving examples)

options.feedback: i.e. means “that is”, introducing an explanation, not examples.

items.explain: e.g. (exempli gratia) = for example; i.e. (id est) = that is.
items.hook: e.g. = example given; i.e. = in essence.

items.prompt: Which word fits? “Don’t ___ the thread in the labyrinth.”

options.feedback: Loose (rhymes with goose) means not tight.

items.explain: Lose = mislay; loose = not tight.
items.hook: Lose lost an o.

items.prompt: In “the ancient, crumbling temple”, what job do “ancient” and “crumbling” do?

options.feedback: “crumbling” looks like a verb, but here it describes the temple.
Adverbs modify verbs; these modify a noun.

items.explain: Pre-modifiers come before the head noun in a noun phrase.
items.hook: Pre = before: pre-modifiers come before the noun, like an opening act.

items.prompt: In “the temple on the hill”, what is “on the hill”?

options.text: a prepositional phrase post-modifying the noun
the main verb of the noun phrase
options.feedback: There is no verb in this phrase.

options.text: a subordinate clause pre-modifying the noun
options.feedback: A clause needs a verb.

items.explain: Post-modifiers come after the noun: prepositional phrases or relative clauses.
items.hook: Post = after: post-modifiers come after the noun, like a PS after a letter.

items.prompt: “Medusa, a Gorgon with snakes for hair, lived alone.” What is “a Gorgon with snakes for hair”?

options.feedback: There is no relative pronoun like who or which.
It is one phrase describing Medusa.

items.explain: Apposition places two noun phrases side by side, the second renaming the first.
items.example: News reports use apposition constantly: “Big Ben, the Great Bell of Westminster, rang out.”

items.prompt: “Gripping the thread, Theseus entered the labyrinth.” What is “Gripping the thread”?

options.text: a main clause with a subject
options.feedback: It cannot stand alone: it has no subject and its verb has no tense.

options.text: a noun phrase acting as subject
options.feedback: It describes what Theseus is doing; “Theseus” is the subject.

items.explain: Non-finite clauses (-ing or -ed openers) add action without starting a new sentence.
items.hook: Non-finite = no tense and no subject: “Gripping the thread” needs a main clause to finish it.

items.prompt: Which sentence contains a dangling modifier (an opener attached to the wrong noun)?

options.text: Walking into the cave, the smell hit Theo.
Walking into the cave, Theo noticed the smell.
options.feedback: Here Theo is walking: correct.

options.text: As Theo walked into the cave, the smell hit him.
options.feedback: The subordinate clause makes it clear: correct.

items.explain: The opener must describe the subject that follows it. The smell was not walking.
items.example: A classic howler: “Walking to school, a tree fell on me.” Was the tree walking?

items.prompt: What is the effect of “Into the darkness crept the Minotaur”, compared with “The Minotaur crept into the darkness”?

options.text: The monster is delayed to the end, building suspense
It is ungrammatical, because the verb comes first
options.feedback: Inversion is a deliberate, correct structure.

options.text: It makes the Minotaur the object of the sentence
options.feedback: The Minotaur is still the subject: it is still the one doing the creeping.

items.explain: Inversion changes normal word order to control what the reader meets first and last.
items.example: “Down came the rain” and “Here comes the bride” both put the verb before the subject.

items.prompt: A writer follows a long descriptive paragraph with: “Silence.” What is this, and why use it?

options.text: A minor sentence, for sudden emphasis

options.feedback: It is deliberate.

options.text: A complete main clause for emphasis
options.feedback: It has no verb, so it cannot be a main clause.

items.explain: Minor sentences break the rules on purpose for impact.
items.hook: A minor sentence is a pause made solid: a word or two, then a full stop.

items.prompt: Which is a periodic sentence (the main clause is held back until the end)?

options.text: Through the storm, past the rocks and beneath the cliffs, Odysseus finally reached home.
Odysseus finally reached home, after the storm, the rocks and the cliffs.
options.feedback: The main clause comes first: a loose sentence.

options.text: Odysseus reached home and he was tired, for the voyage had been long.
options.feedback: A compound sentence with the main clause first.

items.explain: Periodic sentences create suspense by delaying the main point.
items.hook: In a periodic sentence the point arrives only at the full stop, which Americans call a period.

items.prompt: “He ran and he fell and he rose and he ran again.” What is this technique, and its effect?

options.text: Asyndeton: leaving out conjunctions for speed
options.feedback: There are many conjunctions here.
No opposite ideas are being balanced here.

items.explain: Polysyndeton (many conjunctions) slows or intensifies; asyndeton (none) speeds up.
items.hook: Poly = many: many “and”s, a breathless pile-up.

items.prompt: “She was tired, cold, hungry, afraid.” What does the asyndetic list (no “and”) suggest?

options.text: The feelings pile up quickly and seem endless
The list is unfinished because the writer made a mistake
options.feedback: Leaving out “and” is deliberate.

options.text: She feels calm and in control
options.feedback: Look at the words themselves.

items.explain: Without a final “and”, a list feels open-ended and overwhelming.
items.example: Shopping lists are naturally asyndetic: eggs, milk, bread, butter.

items.prompt: Why might a writer choose “Slowly, the door opened” rather than “The door opened slowly”?

options.text: It puts the emphasis on how it happened
The second version is grammatically wrong
options.feedback: Both are correct; the choice is about emphasis.

options.text: It makes “slowly” the subject of the sentence
options.feedback: The door is the subject in both.

items.explain: Fronted adverbials put the manner, time or place in the spotlight.
items.hook: Whatever comes first gets the spotlight.

items.prompt: A politician says “Mistakes were made.” Why might the passive be chosen here?

options.text: It hides who made the mistakes

options.feedback: It actually gives less information.

options.text: It is written in the future tense
options.feedback: “were made” is past.

items.explain: The passive can leave out the agent, avoiding blame.
items.hook: The zombie test: “Mistakes were made (by zombies).” If zombies fit, it is passive.

items.prompt: When the weather or setting reflects a character’s mood, it is called…
items.explain: From Greek pathos (feeling): the storm rages as the hero despairs.
items.hook: Pathos = feeling: the weather seems to share the characters’ feelings.

items.prompt: A repeated image or idea that carries meaning through a story is a…
items.explain: The thread in the labyrinth could be a motif for hope or guidance.
items.example: In many films a piece of music returns whenever one character appears: a musical motif.

items.prompt: A hint early in a story of what will happen later is called…
items.explain: Oracles in myths are pure foreshadowing.
items.example: The witches’ prophecies in Macbeth foreshadow almost everything that follows.

items.prompt: A story whose ending deliberately echoes or returns to its opening has a… structure.
items.explain: A cyclical structure can suggest closure, or that nothing can escape fate.
items.hook: Cyclical = cycle: wheel back to the start, then notice what has changed.

items.prompt: A narrator whose account the reader cannot fully trust is called…
items.explain: Look for contradictions, boasting, or other characters reacting differently.
items.hook: Spot the unreliable narrator: contradictions, boasting, and others who see it differently.

items.prompt: Homer’s Odyssey opens ten years after the war, with Odysseus already stranded. Starting in the middle of the action is called…
items.explain: Latin for “into the middle of things”. The earlier adventures are told later as flashbacks.

items.prompt: A scene that jumps back to an earlier time is a…
items.explain: Odysseus tells his earlier adventures to the Phaeacians as a long flashback.
items.example: In Books 9 to 12 of the Odyssey, Odysseus tells the Phaeacians about the Cyclops, Circe and the Sirens.

items.prompt: When the audience knows something a character does not (Oedipus searching for the killer who is himself), it is called…
items.explain: Dramatic irony creates tension: we watch characters walk towards a truth we already know.
items.hook: Dramatic irony: we know, they do not.

items.prompt: The narrator says “he”, but we only see what Theo sees and thinks. What kind of narration is this?

options.feedback: First person would use “I”.
An omniscient narrator would know everyone’s thoughts.

items.explain: Third person limited keeps us close to one character while keeping some distance.
items.hook: Third person limited: a camera on one character’s shoulder.

items.prompt: In the myth, Ariadne’s thread leads Theseus out of the labyrinth. What could it symbolise?

options.text: hope, love or a way out of danger

options.feedback: The thread helps Theseus escape.
Objects in stories often carry symbolic meaning.

items.explain: A symbol is an object that stands for an idea. Good analysis offers an interpretation and supports it.
items.example: The word “clue” comes from “clew”, a ball of thread, after the thread that led Theseus out of the labyrinth.

items.prompt: In a mystery, a false clue that leads the reader the wrong way is a…
items.explain: Detective writers like Conan Doyle use red herrings to keep readers guessing.
items.hook: A red herring is a strong-smelling false trail: it leads the reader the wrong way.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses pathetic fallacy?

options.text: The sky darkened and the rain began to weep as the funeral started.
The funeral started at noon, and everyone wore black.
options.feedback: There is no weather reflecting mood.

options.text: She was as sad as a wilted flower left in the rain.
options.feedback: That is a simile about her, not weather reflecting mood.

items.explain: The weeping rain mirrors the mourners’ grief.

items.prompt: A story opens and closes with the same image of an empty beach. What might this cyclical structure suggest?

options.text: That the character is trapped, or has come full circle
That the writer ran out of ideas for a new ending
options.feedback: An echo like this is a deliberate choice.

options.text: That nothing important happened in the story at all
options.feedback: Events happen; the echo makes us compare the start and the end.

items.explain: Cyclical structures invite the reader to notice what has, and has not, changed.

items.prompt: An opening line designed to grab the reader’s attention is called a…
items.explain: Hooks can be a question, a surprising statement, a line of dialogue or action.
items.example: “It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen.” Orwell’s opening is a classic hook.

items.prompt: A description moves from the whole stormy sea, to the ship, to one sailor’s hands. What structure is this?

options.feedback: There is no jump back in time.

options.text: a list of what is there
options.feedback: It is a deliberate shift of focus.

items.explain: Moving from wide to close focus guides the reader’s eye, as a film director would.
items.hook: Wide shot, mid shot, close-up: write like a camera zooming in.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest description?

options.text: The wolf walked in a quiet and menacing way.
options.feedback: A precise verb does the job of the whole phrase.

options.text: The wolf walked very, very quietly.
options.feedback: Intensifiers like “very” are weak.

items.explain: A precise verb beats an ordinary verb plus adverbs.
items.hook: One sharp verb beats a blunt verb with adverbs: prowled, crept, stalked.

items.prompt: Why is “the gnarled olive tree” better than “the old tree”?

options.text: A precise noun and adjective create a clear picture
It is longer, so it gives the reader more to read
options.feedback: Length is not the point: precision is.

options.text: Olive trees are more important in Greek myths
options.feedback: It is about specific detail.

items.explain: Specific nouns (olive, cypress, oak) let the reader see exactly what you see.
items.hook: Name it precisely: not “tree” but oak, olive or yew.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses a sense other than sight?

options.text: The sea was a deep blue.
options.feedback: That is sight.

options.text: The cliffs were tall and grey.
options.feedback: That is sight.

items.explain: Taste, touch, smell and sound make description vivid and immersive.
items.hook: Go beyond sight: what can you hear, smell, taste and touch?

items.prompt: Which phrase is a cliché best avoided?

options.text: as cold as the inside of a tomb
options.feedback: This is fresher and fits a gothic mood.

options.text: the wind sliced through her coat
options.feedback: A vivid, original verb.

items.explain: Clichés are so familiar the reader stops seeing them.
items.hook: If you have heard it a hundred times, so has your reader: find a fresh comparison.
items.example: Common clichés: “as cold as ice”, “as good as gold”, “at the end of the day”.

items.prompt: A writer describes a city as a beast throughout: its streets are veins, its traffic growls, its towers are teeth. This is…

options.feedback: It runs through the whole description, and there is no “like” or “as”.
Only “growls” suggests a sound.

items.explain: An extended metaphor sustains one comparison across a passage.

items.prompt: Why might a descriptive piece be written in the present tense?

options.text: It creates immediacy, as if the reader is there now
It is required in all descriptive writing
options.feedback: Most stories use the past tense.

options.text: It makes the writing shorter and easier to read
options.feedback: Tense does not affect length.

items.explain: The present tense can make a moment feel vivid and urgent.
items.example: Live sports commentary is in the present tense: “He shoots… he scores!”

items.prompt: Which sentence shows rather than tells that Mira is nervous?

options.text: Mira twisted the strap of her bag until her knuckles whitened.
Mira was very nervous about what would happen next.
options.feedback: That tells us directly.

options.text: Mira felt nervous, anxious and unsure of herself.
options.feedback: Three telling words are still telling.

items.explain: Showing gives the reader evidence and lets them infer the emotion.
items.hook: Show the body: whitening knuckles say “nervous” without the word.

items.prompt: “Beneath the bright festival lanterns, a beggar shivered in the shadows.” What technique creates the effect?

options.text: contrast of light and dark, wealth and poverty

options.feedback: Look at the opposites placed side by side.
The lanterns are not given human qualities; look at the opposites placed side by side.

items.explain: Placing opposites together sharpens both.
items.hook: Light beside dark makes both stronger, like a candle in a black room.

items.prompt: A strong way to end a descriptive piece is to…

options.text: return to an image from the opening, now changed
write “The end” so the reader knows it has finished
options.feedback: Let the final image do the work.

options.text: list everything that was described again
options.feedback: Repetition of the whole is weak; one echoed image is powerful.

items.explain: A changed echo of the opening gives a sense of shape and closure.
items.hook: End with an echo: return to the opening image, now changed.

items.prompt: A formal letter begins “Dear Sir or Madam”. How should it end?

options.feedback: Use “sincerely” when you have named the person (Dear Ms Patel).
Far too informal.

items.explain: Unknown name: Yours faithfully. Named person: Yours sincerely.
items.hook: Never put two s’s together: Sir does not go with sincerely. Dear Sir or Madam → Yours faithfully.

items.prompt: A letter begins “Dear Mr Hughes”. How should it end?

options.feedback: That is for “Dear Sir or Madam”.
Too informal for a formal letter.

items.explain: Named person: Yours sincerely.
items.hook: Named person → sincerely. Unnamed “Sir or Madam” → faithfully.

items.prompt: In a newspaper article, the short summary in bold beneath the headline is called the…
items.explain: The headline grabs attention; the standfirst summarises; the byline names the writer.
items.hook: The standfirst stands first, under the headline, and sums the story up.

items.prompt: The line in an article that names the writer is the…
items.explain: “By Mira Andreou, Education Correspondent”.
items.hook: Byline = the line that says who it is by.

items.prompt: Which feature belongs especially to a speech?

options.feedback: Subheadings suit leaflets and reports; listeners cannot see them.
That belongs to research writing.

items.explain: Speeches are written for the ear: direct address, repetition and rhythm.
items.example: Great speeches are written for the ear: “I have a dream” works because it is heard.

items.prompt: Which sentence is most typical of a review?

options.text: The second act drags, but the final scene is unforgettable.
The play is on at the Globe on Saturday evening at eight.
options.feedback: That is information, not evaluation.

options.text: The play was written by Shakespeare in about 1600.
options.feedback: Reviews evaluate; this just states a fact.

items.explain: Reviews use evaluative language and give a balanced judgement.
items.example: The star rating at the top of a film review sums up its judgement in a glance.

items.prompt: Which is most typical of a formal report?

options.text: an impersonal tone, subheadings and recommendations
rhetorical questions to grab the reader in every paragraph
options.feedback: That suits a speech or article.
Reports are impersonal.

items.explain: Reports inform and recommend: impersonal, organised, precise.
items.hook: Reports: headings, facts, an impersonal tone and recommendations. No drama.

items.prompt: What is the difference between writing to argue and writing to persuade?

options.text: An argument weighs both sides; persuasion pushes one view
Persuasion weighs both sides; an argument pushes one view
options.feedback: They overlap, but argument considers the other side more fully.

options.text: There is no difference: both just give your opinion
options.feedback: A good argument is calm and reasoned.

items.explain: Exam tasks often blend them, but the best answers acknowledge and rebut the other side.
items.hook: Argue = weigh both sides; persuade = push one side.

items.prompt: Before writing any non-fiction task, which three things should you identify?

options.feedback: Those matter less than who you are writing for and why.
Important, but they come after you know your task.

items.explain: Form, audience and purpose decide your register, structure and devices.
items.hook: PAF: Purpose, Audience, Form. Ask all three before you write.

items.prompt: Compared with a tabloid, a broadsheet article is usually…

options.text: more formal, with longer sentences and fewer puns
shorter, with more slang and bigger headlines
options.feedback: That describes many tabloids.

options.text: written only in the first person, like a diary
options.feedback: Most news writing is third person.

items.explain: Register shifts with the publication and its readers.
items.example: Broadsheets were named after their large pages, though many are now printed in a smaller size.

items.prompt: Where is a counter-argument most effectively placed in a persuasive article?

options.text: near the end, followed by a strong rebuttal
in the very first sentence, before anything else
options.feedback: Open with your own hook and view.
Addressing it makes you more convincing.

items.explain: Acknowledge, then rebut: “Some argue… However…”
items.hook: Acknowledge, then rebut: “Some argue… However…”

items.prompt: Which is an opinion rather than a fact?

options.text: The Parthenon is the most beautiful building ever made.
The Parthenon was completed in 432 BC.
options.feedback: That is a checkable fact.

options.text: The Parthenon stands on the Acropolis, a hill above Athens.
options.feedback: That is a fact.

items.explain: Facts can be checked; opinions are judgements.
items.hook: If you could look it up and prove it, it is a fact.

items.prompt: Which features would you expect in an information leaflet?

options.text: headings, short sections and bullet points
a rhyming scheme and regular rhythm
options.feedback: That belongs to poetry.
Leaflets present information clearly and briefly.

items.explain: Leaflets are designed for skimming: clear headings and short chunks.
items.hook: Leaflets are built for skimming: headings, bullet points, short chunks.

items.prompt: A travel blog is usually…

options.text: personal and chatty, in the first person
strictly impersonal and formal, like a report
options.feedback: Blogs are usually personal.

options.text: written as a play script with stage directions
options.feedback: Blogs are prose.

items.explain: Blogs blend information with a personal voice.
items.hook: Blog is short for “weblog”: a log, or diary, kept on the web.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “careful and hard-working”.
items.explain: conscientious. conscien(ce) + -tious, dropping the final -ce: a conscientious worker listens to her conscience.
items.learn: **conscientious** (careful and hard-working). conscien(ce) + -tious, dropping the final -ce: a conscientious worker listens to her conscience.
items.example: School reports often praise a “conscientious” pupil: careful and hard-working.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “an expert judge of fine things”.
items.explain: connoisseur. Double n, double s, and “eu” near the end: con-nois-seur.
items.learn: **connoisseur** (an expert judge of fine things). Double n, double s, and “eu” near the end: con-nois-seur.
items.hook: Connoisseur comes from an old French word for “one who knows”.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “general agreement”.
items.explain: consensus. It comes from “consent”, not “census”: con-sen-sus.
items.learn: **consensus** (general agreement). It comes from “consent”, not “census”: con-sen-sus.
items.hook: Consensus is about consent (agreeing), not a census (counting).

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “completely dried out”.
items.explain: desiccated. One s, two c’s: a desert is dry and has one s.
items.learn: **desiccated** (completely dried out). One s, two c’s: a desert is dry and has one s.
items.example: Desiccated coconut, the dried flakes used in baking, has the spelling on every packet.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a difficult choice between two options”.
items.explain: dilemma. di (two) + lemma: double m, no n.
items.learn: **dilemma** (a difficult choice between two options). di (two) + lemma: double m, no n.
items.hook: A dilemma has two horns, so it has two m’s.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “overwhelming happiness”.
items.explain: ecstasy. Ends -asy, like “fantasy”: ec-sta-sy.
items.learn: **ecstasy** (overwhelming happiness). Ends -asy, like “fantasy”: ec-sta-sy.
items.hook: From Greek ekstasis, “standing outside yourself”: so happy you are beside yourself.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “glowing brightly”.
items.explain: fluorescent. “fluor” as in fluoride, then -escent.
items.learn: **fluorescent** (glowing brightly). “fluor” as in fluoride, then -escent.
items.hook: Fluor- as in fluoride toothpaste: f-l-u-o-r, not flour.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “to pester or intimidate repeatedly”.
items.explain: harass. One r, two s’s: har-ass.
items.learn: **harass** (to pester or intimidate repeatedly). One r, two s’s: har-ass.
items.hook: Harass: one r, two s’s. Embarrass: two r’s, two s’s.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “an odd personal habit”.
items.explain: idiosyncrasy. It ends -crasy (from Greek krasis, a mixture), not -cracy (rule).
items.learn: **idiosyncrasy** (an odd personal habit). It ends -crasy (from Greek krasis, a mixture), not -cracy (rule).
items.hook: Idio = your own (as in idiom): your own peculiar mixture.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “to vaccinate”.
items.explain: inoculate. One n, one c, one l: in-oc-u-late.
items.learn: **inoculate** (to vaccinate). One n, one c, one l: in-oc-u-late.
items.hook: Inoculate comes from Latin oculus, eye: gardeners once grafted a bud, or “eye”, into a plant.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a skilful movement”.
items.explain: manoeuvre. British spelling: man-oeu-vre.
items.learn: **manoeuvre** (a skilful movement). British spelling: man-oeu-vre.
items.hook: Manoeuvre comes, through French, from Latin for working by hand: man-oeu-vre.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “extremely small”.
items.explain: minuscule. From “minus”, not “mini”: minus-cule.
items.learn: **minuscule** (extremely small). From “minus”, not “mini”: minus-cule.
items.hook: Minuscule comes from minus (less), not mini: minus-cule.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a ruler of ancient Egypt”.
items.explain: pharaoh. The letters go a-o-h at the end: phar-a-oh.
items.learn: **pharaoh** (a ruler of ancient Egypt). The letters go a-o-h at the end: phar-a-oh.
items.hook: Pharaoh ends like a sigh: a, o, h.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a person who writes plays”.
items.explain: playwright. A wright is a maker, as in shipwright: a playwright makes plays.
items.learn: **playwright** (a person who writes plays). A wright is a maker, as in shipwright: a playwright makes plays.
items.example: Shipwrights build ships and wheelwrights make wheels; playwrights make plays.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “to take the place of something older”.
items.explain: supersede. The only common English word ending in -sede.
items.learn: **supersede** (to take the place of something older). The only common English word ending in -sede.
items.hook: Supersede comes from Latin sedere, to sit: to sit above. It is the only common word ending -sede.

items.prompt: Spell the word that means “a system of government run by officials”.
items.explain: bureaucracy. bureau (desk) + -cracy (Greek kratos, power).
items.learn: **bureaucracy** (a system of government run by officials). bureau (desk) + -cracy (Greek kratos, power).
items.hook: Bureau is French for desk: bureaucracy is rule by people at desks.

items.prompt: “Theo stared at the door. Why had he agreed to this? It was madness, all of it.” What is this technique?

options.feedback: It uses “he”, not “I”.
There are no speech marks: these are thoughts.

items.explain: Free indirect style blends the narrator’s voice with a character’s, bringing us close to their mind.
items.hook: Free indirect style: third-person words, first-person thoughts.
items.example: Jane Austen is famous for it: in Emma, the narrator slips in and out of Emma’s own thoughts.

items.prompt: The term “focalisation” in a story refers to…

options.text: whose perspective the events are seen through
the most important event in the plot
options.feedback: That is the climax.

options.text: the setting where the main action happens
options.feedback: Focalisation is about point of view.

items.explain: A story narrated in the third person can still be focalised through one character.
items.hook: Focalisation = the focus: whose eyes is the camera looking through?

items.prompt: A fire station burns down. What kind of irony is this?

options.feedback: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows more than a character.
Verbal irony is saying the opposite of what you mean.

items.explain: Situational irony: the outcome is the opposite of what we expect. It lies in the events themselves.
items.example: A traffic warden getting a parking ticket is situational irony.

items.prompt: Soaked by the storm, Kit says, “Lovely weather for a voyage.” This is…

options.feedback: No one is missing information.
The weather is real; the irony is in his words.

items.explain: Verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant.
items.hook: Verbal irony: the words say one thing; the meaning is the opposite.

items.prompt: “He fought the Hydra, defeated the lion of Nemea, and then tripped over his own sandal.” What is the effect called?

options.feedback: Pathos is sadness or pity.
The effect comes from the anticlimax.

items.explain: Bathos is a comic drop from the grand to the trivial: it deliberately deflates a serious build-up.
items.hook: Bathos is Greek for depth: a sudden tumble from the grand to the ridiculous.

items.prompt: Which clue most suggests a narrator is unreliable?

options.text: other characters contradict the narrator’s account
the narrator uses long, complicated sentences
options.feedback: Style alone does not make a narrator untrustworthy.

options.text: the narrator describes the weather in great detail
options.feedback: That is ordinary description.

items.explain: Contradictions between what the narrator tells us and what we see are the key evidence.

items.prompt: A story begins: “You open the door. You should not have opened the door.” What is the effect of second-person narration?

options.text: it pulls the reader into the action, making them complicit
it makes the story more formal and distant from us
options.feedback: It is more intimate, not more formal.

options.text: it shows the narrator is lying to the other characters
options.feedback: It is about involving the reader.

items.explain: Second person is rare and striking, often unsettling.

items.prompt: An omniscient narrator…

options.text: knows the thoughts and feelings of every character
is always one of the characters inside the story
options.feedback: Omniscient narrators usually stand outside the story.

options.text: only describes what can be seen and heard
options.feedback: They can reveal everything.

items.explain: From Latin omni (all) + sciens (knowing).

items.prompt: Frankenstein opens with Captain Walton’s letters to his sister. A story told through letters or documents is…

options.feedback: An allegory has a hidden moral meaning.
Letters give one limited voice at a time.

items.explain: Epistolary novels feel personal and immediate, but each letter-writer has a limited view.
items.hook: An epistle is a letter, as in the Epistles of the Bible: epistolary stories are told in letters.
items.example: Dracula is told through diaries, letters and newspaper cuttings.

items.prompt: A story in which characters and events stand for bigger ideas (such as Plato’s cave standing for ignorance and knowledge) is an…

options.feedback: An anecdote is a short real story.
An epilogue comes at the end of a work.

items.explain: Plato’s Allegory of the Cave is one of the most famous in Western thought.
items.example: Orwell’s Animal Farm is an allegory of the Russian Revolution.

items.prompt: Which of these is a STRUCTURAL feature rather than a language feature?

options.text: a shift from the present to a memory

options.feedback: Similes are language features.
Alliteration is a sound device: language.

items.explain: Structure is about order, focus and pace across the whole text.
items.hook: Language = the words; structure = the order and shape of the whole.

items.prompt: A text begins with a wide view of a burning city, then focuses on a single child holding a toy. Why might the writer make this shift?

options.text: to move from the disaster’s scale to its human cost
because the writer forgot about the city
options.feedback: The shift is deliberate.

options.text: to confuse the reader about where we are
options.feedback: It guides, not confuses.

items.explain: Structural shifts in focus direct the reader’s emotions.
items.hook: From wide to close: the crowd, then the face. The scale, then the person.

items.prompt: The writer does not reveal what is in the box until the final paragraph. This technique is…

options.text: a flashback to an earlier time
options.feedback: There is no jump in time.
It is the opposite: holding back.

items.explain: Delaying a reveal keeps the reader reading.
items.example: TV quiz shows withhold the answer: “The winner is… after the break!”

items.prompt: A writer spends three paragraphs on one minute of a fight, then summarises the next ten years in one sentence. What is being controlled?

options.feedback: Both parts could be in the same tense.
The narrator stays the same.

items.explain: Writers stretch time for what matters most.
items.hook: Slow down for what matters; skip what does not.

items.prompt: Which is the best way to begin writing about structure in an exam answer?

options.text: “At the start, the writer focuses on…, before shifting to… in order to…”
“The writer uses lots of nice words and some long sentences.”
options.feedback: That is vague and about language, not structure.

options.text: “The text has paragraphs, which makes it easier to read.”
options.feedback: True of every text: say what the arrangement achieves.

items.explain: Track the text’s movement and explain the purpose of each shift.

items.prompt: Why might a writer place a one-sentence paragraph just after a long, dense one?

options.text: to create a sudden contrast that gives it emphasis
to save space on the page for the next part
options.feedback: It is about impact.

options.text: because they ran out of ideas for that paragraph
options.feedback: It is a deliberate structural choice.

items.explain: Paragraph length is part of structure.
items.hook: A one-line paragraph after a dense one is a spotlight.

items.prompt: Ending a chapter just before a crucial event is resolved is called a…

options.feedback: The opposite: nothing is resolved.
A prologue comes at the beginning.

items.explain: Cliffhangers create suspense across chapters.
items.hook: A cliffhanger leaves the hero hanging off a cliff, and the reader hanging on.
items.example: TV soaps end episodes on cliffhangers so that viewers tune in next time.

items.prompt: What does a sudden burst of short lines of dialogue usually do to the pace?

options.feedback: Short exchanges move quickly down the page.
Layout affects how fast we read.

items.explain: Rapid dialogue creates urgency or conflict.

items.prompt: One chapter ends with a wedding; the next opens with a funeral. What structural technique is this?

options.feedback: Nothing hints at the future here; the contrast is immediate.
There is no jump back in time.

items.explain: Placing contrasting scenes side by side sharpens both.
items.hook: Juxta = next to: put a wedding next to a funeral and both hit harder.

items.prompt: Which opening technique begins with characters already speaking?

options.feedback: That begins with place.
That jumps ahead in time.

items.explain: Dialogue openings drop the reader straight into relationships and conflict.

items.prompt: “Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.” (Kennedy) What device is this?

options.feedback: Look at the word order, not the sounds.
No sound words here.

items.explain: Chiasmus (from the Greek letter chi, X) crosses the structure: A B, B A.
items.hook: Chi is the Greek letter X: the words cross over, A B, B A.
items.example: “When the going gets tough, the tough get going” is an everyday chiasmus.

items.prompt: “…government of the people, by the people, for the people.” (Lincoln) Which device repeats words at the END of phrases?

options.feedback: Anaphora repeats words at the START.
Litotes is understatement.

items.explain: Epistrophe: repetition at the end; anaphora: at the beginning.
items.hook: Anaphora at the start, epistrophe at the end.
items.example: Lincoln spoke these words at Gettysburg in 1863, in a speech of only about 270 words.

items.prompt: “What made Athens great? Not its walls, but its citizens.” What is this device?

options.feedback: This question is answered straight away.
Zeugma uses one word in two senses.

items.explain: Hypophora means asking a question and answering it yourself; it lets the speaker control the argument.
items.hook: Hypophora: ask it, then answer it yourself. You control the debate.

items.prompt: Describing the Trojan War as “not a small quarrel” is an example of…

options.feedback: Hyperbole exaggerates; this understates.
Antithesis balances opposites.

items.explain: Litotes is understatement using a negative (“not a small quarrel”). It can sound modest or ironic, and often makes a point more forcefully.
items.example: Everyday litotes: “not bad” for good, “not the worst idea” for a good one.

items.prompt: “He took his hat and his leave.” What is the device?

options.feedback: There are only two items.
Nothing is reversed.

items.explain: Zeugma uses one verb (here “took”) in two different senses, creating wit.
items.example: A zeugma joke: “She lost her keys and her temper.”

items.prompt: “O Death, where is thy sting?” Addressing someone absent or something abstract is called…

options.feedback: Same word, different meaning: this is a rhetorical device, not punctuation.
It is an address, not a self-answered question.

items.explain: Apostrophe (Greek, “turning away”) addresses the absent, the dead or ideas.
items.example: “Twinkle, twinkle, little star, how I wonder what you are” uses apostrophe: it talks to a star.

items.prompt: “I came, I saw, I conquered.” (Julius Caesar) Which two devices does this combine?

options.feedback: There are no conjunctions at all.
Look at the missing “and” and the three parts.

items.explain: In Latin: veni, vidi, vici. Speed and confidence in three beats.
items.hook: Veni, vidi, vici: no “and”, three beats, total confidence.

items.prompt: “Some will say that the old library is too expensive to save. But consider what we lose if it closes.” What is the device?

options.feedback: Nothing is exaggerated.
No absent person is addressed.

items.explain: Procatalepsis means anticipating an objection and answering it. Raising the opponent’s best argument first makes you seem fair, and lets you shape the reply.
items.hook: Pro (before) + katalepsis (seizing): grab the objection before your opponent can.

items.prompt: Greek rhetoric also prized “kairos”. What is it?

options.text: choosing the right moment to make an argument
a type of metaphor used in speeches
options.feedback: It is about timing.

options.text: the speaker’s honesty and good character
options.feedback: That is closer to ethos.

items.explain: A brilliant speech at the wrong moment can fail: kairos is timing.
items.hook: Kairos = the right moment: a joke at a funeral fails, however clever it is.

items.prompt: “I have told you a thousand times!” is an example of…

options.feedback: Litotes understates.
It is not meant literally.

items.explain: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. From Greek hyper (over) + ballein (to throw): throwing beyond.

items.prompt: “Pride leads to anger. Anger leads to war.” A phrase that begins with the word that ended the last one is…

options.feedback: Epistrophe repeats endings at the end.
Zeugma is one word with two senses.

items.explain: Anadiplosis builds a chain, each step leading to the next.
items.hook: Anadiplosis: the last word of one phrase becomes the first of the next, like links in a chain.

items.prompt: Arranging ideas in order of increasing importance, ending on the strongest, is called…

options.feedback: Anticlimax drops away at the end.
A digression wanders away from the point.

items.explain: Climax is a rhetorical build-up to the strongest point. From Greek klimax, a ladder.
items.hook: Klimax is Greek for ladder: climb rung by rung to the strongest point.

sentences.title: Inversion
sentences.prompt: Write ONE sentence that begins with where something happens and delays the subject to the end, like “Into the cave crept…”.

checks.msg: Start with a place word such as Into, Through, Beneath or Across.
Write a full sentence.

sentences.model: Into the silent labyrinth crept the hero.
sentences.tip: Put the setting first and the subject last to build suspense.

sentences.title: A minor sentence for impact
sentences.prompt: Write two sentences: a longer one describing a storm at sea, then a minor sentence of one to three words.

checks.msg: End with a very short second sentence of one to three words.
Make the first sentence a full description.

sentences.model: The waves rose higher than the mast and tore the sail from its ropes. Then nothing.
sentences.tip: A minor sentence has no main verb; its shortness gives it force.

sentences.title: An asyndetic list
