sentences.prompt: Describe the inside of a monster’s cave with a list of at least four things, separated by commas, with NO “and”.

checks.msg: List at least four things separated by commas.
Leave out “and” completely.

sentences.model: The cave was full of bones, rusted helmets, broken shields, rotting fleeces.
sentences.tip: Without “and”, a list feels endless and overwhelming.

sentences.title: Polysyndeton
sentences.prompt: Write ONE sentence about a long journey that uses “and” at least three times on purpose, for a breathless rhythm.

checks.msg: Use “and” at least three times.

sentences.model: They sailed and they rowed and they starved and still they did not reach home.
sentences.tip: Repeating “and” slows the reader and makes the journey feel endless.

sentences.title: Pathetic fallacy
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence in which the weather reflects a character’s sadness or anger. Use a weather word such as rain, storm, wind, cloud, sky, thunder or mist.

checks.msg: Include some weather.
Link the weather to the character’s feeling.

sentences.model: As Penelope wept at the window, the grey sky wept with her.
sentences.tip: The weather mirrors the mood without naming it directly.

sentences.title: Foreshadowing
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that hints at a future disaster, beginning “Later, …”.

checks.msg: Begin with “Later”.
Hint at what will happen, e.g. “she would remember…”.

sentences.model: Later, she would remember that the birds had stopped singing.
sentences.tip: A hint is enough: let the reader fear what is coming.

sentences.title: Apposition
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that names a character from myth and renames them with a noun phrase inside commas, like “Medusa, a Gorgon with snakes for hair, …”.

checks.msg: Name, then a comma, then a phrase starting with the/a/an, then another comma.

sentences.model: Odysseus, the cleverest of the Greeks, tricked the Cyclops with a false name.
sentences.tip: The appositive renames the noun just before it.

sentences.title: A non-finite opener (-ing)
sentences.prompt: Begin a sentence with an -ing clause, followed by a comma and the subject: “Gripping the thread, …”.

checks.msg: Start with an -ing word, then a comma.

sentences.model: Gripping the thread tightly, Theseus stepped into the dark.
sentences.tip: Make sure the subject after the comma is doing the action.

sentences.title: A non-finite opener (-ed)
sentences.prompt: Begin a sentence with a past participle clause, such as “Exhausted by the climb, …”.

checks.msg: Start with an -ed (or -en) word, then a comma.

sentences.model: Exhausted by the long climb, Kit sank onto the temple steps.
sentences.tip: The opener describes the subject that comes after the comma.

sentences.title: Ask and answer
sentences.prompt: Write a question followed by your own answer, as a speaker might: “What makes a hero? …”.

checks.msg: Ask a question, then answer it in a new sentence.

sentences.model: What makes a hero? Not strength, but the choice to be brave.
sentences.tip: Hypophora lets you raise a question and control the answer.

sentences.title: A formal letter opening
sentences.prompt: Write the greeting and first sentence of a formal letter to a museum, beginning “Dear Sir or Madam,”.

checks.msg: Begin with “Dear Sir or Madam,” and a comma.
Use the formal opener “I am writing to…”.
Avoid contractions in formal writing.

sentences.model: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask whether your museum will display the new Greek vases next summer.
sentences.tip: Formal letters avoid contractions and state their purpose straight away.

sentences.title: An alliterative headline
sentences.prompt: Write a newspaper headline about a myth using alliteration (at least two neighbouring words starting with the same letter).

checks.msg: Put two words starting with the same letter next to each other.
Headlines need at least four words.

sentences.model: Panic at the Palace as Poseidon Prowls
sentences.tip: Headlines grab attention with sound patterns and strong verbs.

sentences.title: A balanced review sentence
sentences.prompt: Write one sentence of a review of a book or film that balances praise and criticism using “although”, “while” or “despite”.

checks.msg: Use although, while or despite.
Give both the praise and the criticism.

sentences.model: Although the middle chapters drag, the final battle is the most thrilling scene I have ever read.
sentences.tip: Balanced judgements sound more trustworthy than pure praise.

sentences.title: Semicolons in a complex list
sentences.prompt: After a colon, list three items, each with extra detail, separated by semicolons: “Kit packed three things: …”.

checks.msg: Use a colon, then separate the detailed items with semicolons.

sentences.model: Kit packed three things: a map, drawn by his grandfather; a lamp, still warm; and a ball of red thread.
sentences.tip: When list items contain commas, semicolons keep them apart.

sentences.title: An ellipsis for suspense
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that uses an ellipsis (…) in the middle to create a pause before a reveal.

checks.msg: Put the ellipsis in the middle, with more words after it.

sentences.model: She lifted the lid slowly… and something inside moved.
sentences.tip: The pause makes the reader hold their breath.

sentences.title: Fewer, not less
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that uses “fewer” correctly with something you can count.

checks.msg: Use the word “fewer”.
Do not use “less” in this sentence.

sentences.model: Fewer ships returned from Troy than had set out.
sentences.tip: Fewer for things you can count; less for amounts.

sentences.title: Fear without the word
sentences.prompt: Describe a character’s fear in one or two sentences WITHOUT using the words scared, afraid, frightened, fear or terrified.

checks.msg: Show the fear through the body and actions instead.
Give the reader enough detail to infer the feeling.

sentences.model: Theo’s breath came in short gasps, and the torch shook so hard that the shadows danced on the walls.
sentences.tip: Show the body: breath, hands, heartbeat, voice.

sentences.title: Personify the sea
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence that gives the sea or the waves human or animal actions.

checks.msg: Make the sea (or waves, tide, ocean) your subject.

sentences.model: The hungry sea gnawed at the cliffs and clawed at the little boat.
sentences.tip: Choose verbs that give the sea a personality.

sentences.title: Inclusive pronouns
sentences.prompt: Write a line for a school assembly speech that uses both “you” and “we” (or “us” or “our”).

checks.msg: Speak to the audience directly with “you”.
Include yourself too with “we”, “us” or “our”.

sentences.model: You may think one voice cannot change anything, but together we can change everything.
sentences.tip: Inclusive pronouns make the audience feel part of the cause.

sentences.title: Anaphora
sentences.prompt: Write two or three short sentences (or clauses) that all begin with the same word or words.

checks.msg: Begin the next sentence or clause with the same opening word(s).

sentences.model: We will remember the fallen. We will rebuild the walls. We will rise again.
sentences.tip: Repeated openings give a speech its drumbeat.

sentences.title: Epistrophe
sentences.prompt: Write a sentence with two clauses that END with the same word, like “The gods were silent; the people were silent.”

checks.msg: End two clauses with the same word.

pieces.passage:
Is this a dagger which I see before me,
The handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee:—
I have thee not, and yet I see thee still.
Art thou not, fatal vision, sensible
To feeling as to sight? or art thou but
A dagger of the mind, a false creation,
Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain?
I see thee yet, in form as palpable
As this which now I draw.
Thou marshall’st me the way that I was going;
And such an instrument I was to use.
Mine eyes are made the fools o’ the other senses,
Or else worth all the rest: I see thee still;
And on thy blade and dudgeon gouts of blood,
Which was not so before.—There’s no such thing:
It is the bloody business which informs
Thus to mine eyes.

[…]

Thou sure and firm-set earth,
Hear not my steps, which way they walk, for fear
Thy very stones prate of my whereabout,
And take the present horror from the time,
Which now suits with it.—Whiles I threat, he lives;
Words to the heat of deeds too cold breath gives.

[A bell rings.]

I go, and it is done; the bell invites me.
Hear it not, Duncan, for it is a knell
That summons thee to heaven or to hell.

pieces.passage:
It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils. With an anxiety that almost amounted to agony, I collected the instruments of life around me, that I might infuse a spark of being into the lifeless thing that lay at my feet. It was already one in the morning; the rain pattered dismally against the panes, and my candle was nearly burnt out, when, by the glimmer of the half-extinguished light, I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open; it breathed hard, and a convulsive motion agitated its limbs.

How can I describe my emotions at this catastrophe, or how delineate the wretch whom with such infinite pains and care I had endeavoured to form? His limbs were in proportion, and I had selected his features as beautiful. Beautiful! Great God! His yellow skin scarcely covered the work of muscles and arteries beneath; his hair was of a lustrous black, and flowing; his teeth of a pearly whiteness; but these luxuriances only formed a more horrid contrast with his watery eyes, that seemed almost of the same colour as the dun-white sockets in which they were set, his shrivelled complexion and straight black lips.

The different accidents of life are not so changeable as the feelings of human nature. I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body. For this I had deprived myself of rest and health. I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation; but now that I had finished, the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart. Unable to endure the aspect of the being I had created, I rushed out of the room and continued a long time traversing my bed-chamber, unable to compose my mind to sleep.

What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?
Only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Only the stuttering rifles’ rapid rattle
Can patter out their hasty orisons.
No mockeries now for them; no prayers nor bells,
Nor any voice of mourning save the choirs,—
The shrill, demented choirs of wailing shells;
And bugles calling for them from sad shires.

Shall shine the holy glimmers of goodbyes.
